A few of us are thinking about starting a project in graphical models and causal inference. This is just the first message to get things started.
@Richard Guo @Rajarshi Mukherjee @Rohit Bhattacharya @Zixiao Jolene Wang

This is a bit off-topic, but @Zixiao Jolene Wang can you explain why you used the sepo agent (I think it's this? https://github.com/self-evolving/repo) for the Statlib project? How is it designed, and how is it different from other coding agents (e.g. codex, opencode) and self-improving agent (e.g. hermes)?
There’s already a discussion thread in #general > Discussion: Lean Workspace I think it would be helpful if we move this question there!
I don't have permission to move this out of this channel. Will post a new one there.
Has there been been any developments in the Graphs & Causality project?
@Bo Cowgill the group is working on setting up the architecture for graphs and operations on graphs. We are aiming to upload a first set of codes soon.
Great. Are you pushing to mathlib or statlib?
Statlib

@Rajarshi Mukherjee — on graph architecture: I have a small standalone Lean 4 development of Pearl's do-calculus that might be relevant input.

Design choices: DAGs carry a rank function with rank_strict_mono : edge u v → rank u < rank v, so acyclicity is structural rather than a separate proof obligation. Undirected walks are an inductive type with fwd/bwd constructors recording edge orientation, and d-separation is decided by a state machine threading the incoming orientation through the walk.

Back-door and front-door adjustment are proven sorry-free for finite discrete models on PMF, with an explicit Bool witness model confirming the front-door statement isn't vacuous. dsep_sound (Verma–Pearl) is still open — I've decomposed it into layers via Lauritzen moralisation rather than direct induction over walks.

Not proposing it as-is; the design choices are mine and may not match what you're building. But if the rank/walk/blocking representation is useful as a reference point: https://github.com/Johaan70/PearlDoCalculus

@Johan Magnus Aanderaa Thanks for the message! I was looking through the DAG definition in your repo https://github.com/Johaan70/PearlDoCalculus/blob/main/PearlDoCalculus/DAG.lean and was wondering about the design choice of requiring [DecidableEq V] specifically. Is there a particular reason you want decidable equality on the vertex type at the level of the DAG structure?

Good catch — you're right that the structure itself doesn't use it. DAG only has edge, decEdge, rank and rank_strict_mono, none of which need decidable equality.

It's there because everything I build on top uses Finset V: parents is Finset.univ.filter (fun u => G.edge u v), and the conditioning sets in d-separation are Finset V too. I put the instance at the structure level so I wouldn't have to thread it through every downstream definition. That was convenience, not a principled choice.

Moving it out to the definitions that actually need it would be cleaner, and would let the graph layer work over vertex types without decidable equality. Is that the direction you're going with the Statlib graph API?

@Johan Magnus Aanderaa Thanks for this. The plan (at least what I had in mind) was to start from more general mixed graphs and not make DAGs central to the development. Happy to hear what what others think about this.

That makes sense — ADMGs are where the completeness results live, and starting from mixed graphs avoids a migration later. I have no stake in DAGs being central; I built that way because it was the smallest thing I could get to work.

On the representation: my Walk type records edge orientation per step (fwd/bwd constructors), and blocking threads that orientation through the walk as a state machine. Adding bidirected edges would mean a third constructor and an extra state — the collider clause is where it changes, since a bidirected edge is always a collider at both endpoints. That part looks mechanical.

What I don't know is whether the moralisation argument survives. Lauritzen's route is stated for DAGs, and I used ancestral closure plus the marriage-edge correspondence to get soundness. Whether that generalises to ADMGs, or whether the general case needs a different proof strategy entirely, is beyond what I've looked at.

If it's of any use: the DAG case is done and sorry-free (#print axioms gives only the standard three), so it could serve as a sanity check for whatever the general development produces — if the general soundness theorem specialises correctly to DAGs, that's some evidence it's stated right.

https://github.com/Johaan70/PearlDoCalculus

@Johan Magnus Aanderaa The moralisation argument extends to ADMGs with a generalization (every collider-connected paths becomes a undirected edge), see https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/1467-9469.00323.
Does you Walk allow duplicated vertices? I'm asking because most standard texts use "paths" (walks without duplicated vertices) to define d-separation, but mathematically it's easier to work with general walks in my opinion.
My plan is to convince people to define walks and d-separation using the matrix algebra introduced here: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.15744 (see Section 6.2 for augmentation criterion for m-separation). We still need to have that discussion.

Yes, my Walk is inductive with fwd/bwd constructors and allows repeated vertices. That was deliberate. The moralisation argument I formalised needs it. In Lauritzen's route the collider case produces a marriage edge, and the resulting moral walk can revisit vertices even when the original was a path. I noted it in the file for exactly that reason.
Working with general walks was also easier for the induction, blocking is a state machine threading edge orientation through the walk, and restricting to paths would have meant carrying a no-duplicates invariant through every step.
Thanks for the Richardson reference. I hadn't seen the collider-connected generalisation. If moralisation extends that way, the structure of my soundness proof might survive with the marriage edge construction replaced by the collider-path one.
The matrix algebra approach is new to me and I'll read Section 6.2. One question from the formalisation side. Does the matrix formulation give decidability of separation for free? My current DSeparated quantifies over all walks, which is fine for proofs but not computable. A matrix criterion would presumably fix that.

The matrix formulation allows us to define "types" of walks via polynomials of basic edge matrices (with "addition" being set union and "multiplication" being concatenation). Separability of vertex sets in a graph can then be defined as the corresponding polynomial equating the null set. Is that what you mean by "decidability of separation for free"?

Close, but I was asking something narrower and more implementation-flavoured.
What I meant: my DSeparated Z x y is ∀ p : Walk G x y, Blocked Z p a quantifier over an infinite type, since walks can repeat vertices and have unbounded length. That's fine for proving things, but Lean can't evaluate it. So I can state d-separation facts and prove them by hand, but I can't ask Lean to decide whether a given Z separates x from y in a given graph, and I can't run a check on a concrete example.
If separability reduces to a polynomial in edge matrices equating the null set, that looks like it would be computable for finite graphs , you evaluate the polynomial and check. That's what I meant by "for free": a Decidable instance falls out of the definition rather than needing a separate reachability algorithm and a soundness proof relating it back to the walk quantifier.
But I may be misreading the construction. Does the polynomial have bounded degree for a finite graph, or does the concatenation product need truncation somewhere?

It could be infinite; I should have said “series” instead of “polynomial”. In the second paper above I gave a result that proves the unsurprising result that d-separation via walks is equivalent to the usual definition of d-separation via paths. The proof as you can imagine is not as clean. (Anything with paths is not clean…) That would give you some thing computable?

Yes, that would do it — a path formulation is decidable for finite graphs, since there are finitely many paths to check.

So the trade-off is clear from where I sit: walks give clean proofs but no decidability, paths give decidability but drag a no-duplicates invariant through every step. The equivalence between them is what buys you both, at a one-time cost.
That cost is real in Lean, though. My blocking predicate is a state machine threading edge orientation through the walk, and every case analysis would need the invariant carried alongside. Proving the equivalence would mean doing that once, carefully, which is probably still cheaper than living with the uncleanness everywhere.
For what it's worth, I've been formalising with walks and haven't missed decidability yet. Everything so far is proving facts about a fixed graph, not asking Lean to compute anything. It would start to matter for worked examples, or if someone wanted to run the identification algorithm.
I'll read the equivalence result. Is it stated for ADMGs or DAGs?
@Johan Magnus Aanderaa The whole paper is done for ADMGs, DAGs are treated as special cases.

Thanks. then the equivalence covers what I'm building. I'll read it properly.
One thing that might be relevant to the representation discussion: I finished the soundness fundament for DAGs this week — the joint distribution factorises along a separator at every rank level, verified sorry-free. The Assignment type is a dependent function on a Finset, which turned out to be the single biggest cost in the project. Most of he work went into transport lemmas for moving between provably-equal index sets.
If the matrix formulation avoids that, it's worth something beyond elegance.

@Bo Cowgill Let's continue the discussion in Issue #40 here.

The progress in developing the graphical models in statlib has been slow so we'd be happy to talk to you to find ways to collaborate. What I want to avoid is to repeat what happened in the literature (e.g. between Rubin and Pearl) and develop two separate theories of causality, because I believe potential outcomes and graphs are parts of the same mathematical framework.

You may argue that graphs are not useful for some empirical work (or a lot of empirical work, which I disagree). For example, you can certainly do IV without graphs, but in that example it is clear that a graphical visualization of IV can only help us understand the core assumptions better and understand why IV is different from other approaches (because the graphs are different). Of course for point identification with IV you need further assumptions (homogeneity, monotonicity, etc.), so the graphical approach is far from complete and the richness of potential outcomes is useful. Graphs are less useful for basic DiD but could still be relevant for more complex identification arguments.

Thank you, @Qingyuan Zhao. I agree that graphs are useful, and we should avoid the conflict between the two literatures. I'm open to finding ways to collaborate.

In my view, there's a distinction between (1) saying that potential outcomes and graphs belong to the same broad mathematical framework --- and (2) saying that they must share a single primitive Lean API from the outset. Even if the first is true, the second is a software-design decision.

My narrower claim is that a basic potential-outcomes formalization of IV or DiD does not require a graphical-model API as a dependency.

We do not need to make a decision before concrete applications give us evidence about the abstractions we need. One possible path is to let #41 merge as the small functional layer we have already discussed while the graphical API continues to develop.

We could then use a concrete example (perhaps IV) as a compatibility test after both initial APIs exist. If that exercise reveals a genuinely shared abstraction, we can refactor toward it with evidence from the applications.

Regarding the graphical layer, I am not well-placed to design it. However, I would be happy to discuss compatibility and collaborate on a well-scoped bridge example. I'm also glad to read any of your proposals. Knowing the first two or three graphical results or applications you want the library to support would help identify possible points of connection.

Hi @Bo Cowgill, my view is potential outcome and graphical models (mostly DAGs and ADMGs) are separate components of the theory of graphical causal models. So I agree they do not need to share a single primitive API.

However, what we can do with potential outcomes alone is fairly limited. Some conditional independence is almost immediately needed for it to be useful, even if one just formalizes randomization tests. (Well, it is possible to take the decision theoretic approach cf Philip Dawid, but that doesn't even require potential outcomes...)

Actually I'm more interested in your view on the philosophy; I think we have a lot of freedom in shaping this project. With how fast things are moving with AI-generated lean proofs, I'm rethinking how this project should be done. We initially wanted to build a lean library to help developing causality research and still want to do that, but I'm a bit worried about irresponsible practices and wonder if we can do something about it. The "Graphs & Causality" project is in an interesting position that it is not absurdly difficult but a lot of the proofs are done in natural language, often with gaps. So it's easy to come up with a sloppy but useless formalization of this theory with AI.

My idea is to use this to test different ways of lean formalization (different prompts/references, different LLMs, different agents, different human-AI collaboration strategies) and report the output quality and share the learnings with community. I understand that this may slow progress and may be quite different from how people usually contribute to a library, but I thought if we just push through the usual formalization steps we kind of miss an opportunity to demonstrate good practices of human-AI collaboration. To do this I thought we can first use several meetings to discuss our strategies and first milestones.

What's your thought on this?

@Qingyuan Zhao, there are several distinct points in your message, so I’ll reply to them separately. As you mentioned:

Hi Bo Cowgill, my view is potential outcome and graphical models (mostly DAGs and ADMGs) are separate components of the theory of graphical causal models. So I agree they do not need to share a single primitive API.

It sounds like we agree. Since #41 looks okay to you and does not create a dependency for the graphical work, I suggest merging it while this discussion continues. It is small and revisable, and merging it does not decide how later graphical or identification layers must be built.

Qingyuan Zhao said:

However, what we can do with potential outcomes alone is fairly limited. Some conditional independence is almost immediately needed for it to be useful, even if one just formalizes randomization tests. (Well, it is possible to take the decision theoretic approach cf Philip Dawid, but that doesn't even require potential outcomes...)

I agree that a bare potential-response object is not enough by itself for identification or inference. That is deliberate: #41 supplies only the object on which later structures and assumptions can be stated.

Later modules can add assignment mechanisms, recorded outcomes, consistency, probability, measurability, and independence assumptions. Depending on the formulation, randomization can be introduced through an assignment design rather than taking conditional independence as the primitive.

With those additional layers, potential outcomes support a large part of modern econometrics, including active research questions that could benefit from formalization. I am not trying to prevent anyone from adding graphical or other extensions.

However, I simply do not think every possible extension must be designed before work on concrete potential-outcomes applications can begin. On a related note, overdesign carries its own risk: we may complicate the foundations with generality that no current application needs and that nobody has yet committed to implementing.

Qingyuan Zhao said:

Actually I'm more interested in your view on the philosophy; I think we have a lot of freedom in shaping this project. With how fast things are moving with AI-generated lean proofs, I'm rethinking how this project should be done. We initially wanted to build a lean library to help developing causality research and still want to do that, but I'm a bit worried about irresponsible practices and wonder if we can do something about it. The "Graphs & Causality" project is in an interesting position that it is not absurdly difficult but a lot of the proofs are done in natural language, often with gaps. So it's easy to come up with a sloppy but useless formalization of this theory with AI.

My idea is to use this to test different ways of lean formalization (different prompts/references, different LLMs, different agents, different human-AI collaboration strategies) and report the output quality and share the learnings with community. I understand that this may slow progress and may be quite different from how people usually contribute to a library, but I thought if we just push through the usual formalization steps we kind of miss an opportunity to demonstrate good practices of human-AI collaboration. To do this I thought we can first use several meetings to discuss our strategies and first milestones.

What's your thought on this?

On the AI question, I agree that sloppy formalization is a real risk. If you carry out a study comparing different approaches to AI-assisted formalization, I would be interested to read the results. I do not think completing such a study should become a prerequisite for progress on the library.

My own bias is toward short feedback loops: merge small, incremental, reviewable pieces; use them in applications; and revise them when their limitations become clear. Authors and reviewers should consider possible future applications, but I suggest not letting hypothetical future problems block contributions that pass the current review process. If a reviewer sees a concrete problem with some code --- whether that is AI-generated or otherwise --- they can point to it and ask that it be fixed.

@Bo Cowgill Thanks for sharing your thoughts. I'm not the maintainer of statlib and I would imagine they will merge your #41 soon.

I've been doing a lot of vibe coding with AI agents and learning about software engineering. What I'm getting at is that the documentation is always as important as writing the code itself, and documentation (from planning to testing, including discussion like this) is getting more and more important. I think the statlib maintainers are also figuring out the best balance for this.

Qingyuan Zhao said:

the documentation is always as important as writing the code itself, and documentation (from planning to testing, including discussion like this) is getting more and more important.

Thanks, Qingyuan. I worked in software engineering before my PhD, and I agree w/ your point: clear documentation, testing, and review are important, even moreso now that AI is involved.
@Bo Cowgill @Qingyuan Zhao @Richard Guo #41 has been merged
Thanks to those who reviewed #41. It has now merged. I plan to continue with the next small potential-outcomes layer from #40: unit-level contrasts and finite-population average effects.

hey Bo, wondering what design doc are you thinking about with next small implementation? also I was wondering if we could have an agreed design doc for each lean file and maintain that as the library grows so that people who join later may find it useful. I found this pretty useful for human collaboration.

Zixiao Jolene Wang said:

hey Bo, wondering what design doc are you thinking about with next small implementation?

Something like #40, which was the design doc for #41 (which was just merged). For the next layer, I would open another scoped issue describing the intended declarations, basic results, and what remains out of scope, then take focused feedback through the usual issue and PR process.

also I was wondering if we could have an agreed design doc for each lean file and maintain that as the library grows so that people who join later may find it useful.

I agree that the design rationale should be recorded for future contributors. My preference would be to preserve that discussion in the design issue, as with #40), while keeping the file’s current documentation in its module docstring and declaration docstrings.

A separate maintained design document for every Lean file would duplicate the source documentation and could eventually drift from the implementation.

@Zixiao Jolene Wang I've opened design issue #43 and implementation PR #44 for the next potential-outcomes layer (unit-level contrasts and finite-population average effects). Feedback welcome on either.

Thanks for the careful layering, Bo. One concrete question on #43: when IV identification is added later, the exclusion restriction (instrument affects outcome only through treatment) is most naturally stated as a d-separation condition in a DAG. Is the plan to leave that connection to the graphical layer, or is there a PO-only formulation of exclusion you have in mind for the identification module? I've been formalizing do-calculus in Lean 4 (github.com/Johaan70/PearlDoCalculus) and ran into exactly this boundary — where PO assumptions need graphical primitives to be stated precisely.
IV exclusion restriction is not a d-separation in graph? I’d say it’s lack of certain directed paths. Using potential outcomes it is typically stated as a irrelevance assumption Y(z,a)=Y(a).

Thanks, @Johan Magnus Aanderaa. IV is one of my favorite applications, so I'm glad you raised this. I think the exact IV API belongs in a later design issue, as nothing in #43 requires us to choose it now.

As @Qingyuan Zhao notes, exclusion has a standard potential-outcomes formulation, such as Y(z,a)=Y(z',a), often abbreviated Y(z,a)=Y(a). I therefore do not think a PO identification module needs a graphical dependency. However, it would be valuable to prove a bridge theorem later -- one that relates that PO irrelevance assumption to the appropriate graphical or structural condition. That would be a good concrete compatibility test for the two developments.
